metadata.title: The Routine Content Of Occupations: New Cross-Country Measures Based On PIAAC

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses OECD PIAAC microdata to construct the Routine Intensity Indicator (RII) and then applies the resulting occupation routine-intensity quartile classification to employment data from labour force surveys. For the PIAAC-based descriptive employment shares shown in Figure 1, the authors explicitly state that the employment figures are reweighted to guarantee representativeness, implying the use of PIAAC survey weights in those computations. However, the paper does not report the specific weight variable name(s) or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so the exact weighting implementation cannot be fully audited from the text provided. For the subsequent application to labour force survey employment growth (Figures 2–3), the routine quartile mapping is treated as time-invariant over the period considered, and the paper does not describe additional complex-survey weighting details for those external employment datasets.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this OECD paper does not model cognitive achievement PVs from PIAAC; instead, it constructs an occupation-level routine-intensity measure (RII) from specific PIAAC questionnaire items and then relates routine intensity to skill proxies and employment patterns. Missing-data handling is described for the four routine-intensity components: respondents with missing answers on any of the four questions (Sequentiability, Flexibility, Plan_own, Organise_own) are discarded to avoid artificially low RII values.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study starts from the full PIAAC database (161,707 individuals in 22 OECD countries) but restricts to employed respondents who provide information on occupation and/or sector. Unemployed respondents are discarded because the relevant routine-intensity questions (sequentiability and flexibility) are absent for them. Self-employed individuals are retained. The analytic sample is further reduced by excluding any respondent with missing information on at least one of the four routine-intensity components (Sequentiability, Flexibility, Plan_own, Organise_own), because missing answers would mechanically lower the constructed RII. No censoring is applied to working hours or wages since these are not used in the routine-intensity construction. For the occupation-disaggregation step, PIAAC data for Australia and Finland are noted as not reported at the 3-digit ISCO2008 disaggregation level and are therefore discarded for the 3-digit routine-intensity mapping.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Trade Policy Paper constructs a new cross-country measure of the routine content of occupations, the Routine Intensity Indicator (RII), using OECD PIAAC adult survey responses. The RII is built from four PIAAC questionnaire items capturing how frequently workers can modify task sequences, change task content, plan their own work, and organise their working time; respondents with missing answers on any component are excluded. The paper then aggregates individual RII values to 3-digit ISCO08 occupations using median RII values and classifies occupations into four routine-intensity quartiles (high, medium, low, non-routine) for 20 OECD countries (with Australia and Finland excluded at the 3-digit mapping step). Descriptively, about 46% of employed persons are in non-routine (18%) or low routine-intensive (28%) occupations, with substantial cross-country variation. Finally, it examines associations between routine intensity and workforce skill proxies (including numeracy skills) and finds a negative but not very strong relationship, and it applies the routine classification to labour force survey employment data to show that routine-intensive occupations are less resilient during business-cycle downturns.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive measurement and cross-country comparison paper rather than an empirical ML prediction study: it does not train or evaluate supervised ML models on student-level outcomes. Consequently, fields such as main_findings (structured ML target/predictor performance) and confounders_identified (conceptual predictors for ML) are intentionally left empty. The paper does use statistical index construction (including Cronbach’s alpha and PCA-based weighting) and correlation-based descriptive relationships, but these are not ML predictive-modeling techniques under the extraction rules.
